Day 34 of 100 · Infrastructure Automation

Conditionals in Ansible

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityInfrastructure AutomationPublished journey entry

Conditionals make tasks depend on facts and results, while `failed_when` lets automation define what failure actually means for a command.

Architecture / mental model

fact / registered result → when / failed_when → run, skip or fail task

How it works

`when` controls whether a task executes based on variables, facts or earlier results. This lets one play adapt to the host rather than force every machine through identical operations.

`failed_when` is crucial when a command's return code does not map cleanly to success/failure. A tool can use a non-zero code to mean 'changes found' or another expected state.

The opposite trap also exists: `ignore_errors` can keep a play moving while hiding a failure that should have stopped the operation. Failure semantics should be encoded, not waved away.

Hands-on reference

# Example logic
# failed_when: result.rc not in [0, 2]
# changed_when: result.rc == 2

Verification

Exercise both branches deliberately: one result that should pass and one that should fail. A conditional you only test on the happy path is still a hypothesis.

Field note / gotcha

`ignore_errors` is not recovery logic. It can turn a broken step into a later, harder-to-diagnose failure.

Security considerations

Conditionals often guard privileged or environment-specific tasks. Verify the source variable cannot be trivially manipulated by an untrusted input.

What I learned

Reliable automation defines failure in terms of the tool's real behavior rather than assuming every non-zero code means the same thing.
